questions.question: Which statement is not correct? A chlorine is more electronegative than bromine; B chlorine is more reactive than bromine; C chloride ions are stronger reducing agents than bromide ions; D chloride ions are stronger reducing agents than fluoride ions.
questions.answer: C - chloride ions are stronger reducing agents than bromide ions (this is wrong; bromide is the stronger reducing agent)
steps: A is correct: electronegativity decreases down Group 7, so Cl is more electronegative than Br.
B is correct: chlorine is more reactive (it is a stronger oxidising agent) than bromine.
C is not correct: reducing power of halide ions increases down the group, so Br- is a stronger reducing agent than Cl-.
D is correct: F- is the weakest reducing agent, so Cl- is stronger than F-. Answer C.

questions.question: Which of these is a disproportionation reaction? Options are in the PDF.
questions.answer: The reaction options are not in the text; check the PDF options for a species that is both oxidised and reduced

questions.question: A white solid X gives a red flame. With aqueous silver nitrate and nitric acid it gives a cream precipitate that dissolves in concentrated aqueous ammonia. What is X? A SrBr2, B NaBr, C LiCl, D BaI2.
questions.answer: A - SrBr2
steps: A red flame points to Sr2+ or Li+; NaBr gives yellow and BaI2 gives green, so B and D are ruled out.
A cream precipitate with AgNO3 indicates bromide (AgBr), not chloride (white AgCl).
AgBr dissolves in concentrated ammonia, but AgI does not.
Sr2+ gives a red flame, so X is SrBr2 (A).

questions.question: Potassium chloride reacts with concentrated sulfuric acid producing misty fumes. It can be deduced that: A sulfuric acid is an oxidising agent, B chloride ions are an oxidising agent, C hydrogen chloride is formed, D chlorine is formed.
questions.answer: C - hydrogen chloride is formed
steps: Misty fumes are steamy fumes of HCl gas forming in moist air.
KCl + H2SO4 -> KHSO4 + HCl is a non-redox reaction in which the less volatile acid displaces HCl.
No oxidation of Cl- occurs, so Cl2 is not formed and H2SO4 is not an oxidising agent here.
Answer C.

questions.question: Which products are formed when chlorine is passed through cold, dilute aqueous sodium hydroxide? A NaCl and NaClO, B NaClO and NaClO3, C NaCl and NaClO3, D NaClO and NaClO4.
questions.answer: A - NaCl and NaClO
steps: Cl2 + 2NaOH -> NaCl + NaClO + H2O in the cold.
Chlorine (0) is reduced to Cl- (-1) and oxidised to ClO- (+1): a disproportionation.
Chlorate (NaClO3) forms only when hot and concentrated alkali is used.
Answer A.

questions.question: Potassium iodide reacts with concentrated sulfuric acid. Which of the following is not a product? A H2S, B I2, C S, D SO3.
questions.answer: D - SO3
steps: Concentrated H2SO4 reduces I- to I2, and is itself reduced to H2S, S and SO2.
H2S, I2 and S are all products of this reaction (A, B and C).
SO3 is not formed; sulfur is reduced from +6 to lower oxidation states, not left at +6 as SO3.
Answer D.

questions.topic: Redox Of Silver With Nitric Acid
questions.question: Silver nitrate can be made by warming silver metal with concentrated nitric acid. Show, by reference to oxidation numbers, that this is a redox reaction.
questions.answer: Ag is oxidised from 0 to +1; N is reduced from +5 (in HNO3) to +4 (in NO2), so it is redox
steps: Silver starts as the element, Ag = 0, and ends in AgNO3 as Ag+ = +1.
Its oxidation number increases, so silver is oxidised.
Nitrogen in HNO3 is +5 and in the NO2 by-product it is +4.
Its oxidation number decreases, so nitrogen is reduced: both oxidation and reduction occur, so it is redox.

questions.question: Student A reacted 50.0 cm3 of silver nitrate solution with excess powdered zinc; the maximum temperature rise was 5.2 C (c = 4.18 J g-1 C-1, density 1.00 g cm-3). Calculate the concentration of the silver nitrate solution in mol dm-3.
questions.answer: Needs the enthalpy change for the reaction Zn + 2Ag+ -> Zn2+ + 2Ag, which is not given in the text; check the data book value in the PDF

questions.question: A 50.0 cm3 sample of the same silver nitrate solution was mixed with excess potassium bromide. The AgBr precipitate weighed 5.96 g. Calculate the concentration of silver nitrate in mol dm-3.
questions.answer: 0.635 mol dm-3
steps: Equation: Ag+(aq) + Br-(aq) -> AgBr(s), so 1 mol Ag+ gives 1 mol AgBr.
Moles Ag+ in 50.0 cm3 = 0.0317 mol.
Concentration = 0.0317 / 0.0500 = 0.635 mol dm-3.

questions.topic: Sources Of Error In Concentration Methods
questions.question: Student A's value was lower and student B's value was higher than the data book value. Give a possible reason for each difference.
questions.answer: A (lower): heat is lost to the surroundings, so the temperature rise is underestimated; B (higher): the precipitate is impure or not fully dried, so its mass is too large
steps: Student A's calorimetry measured a smaller temperature rise than the true value.
Heat loss to the surroundings or the polystyrene cup (or incomplete reaction) causes this lower result.
Student B's precipitate mass is too high if it was not dried fully or contained impurities (e.g. excess KBr or other solids).
A higher mass of AgBr gives a higher calculated concentration of AgNO3.

questions.question: Which gas or gases form when sodium fluoride reacts with concentrated sulfuric acid? A hydrogen fluoride only, B hydrogen fluoride and fluorine only, C hydrogen fluoride and sulfur dioxide only, D hydrogen fluoride, fluorine and sulfur dioxide only.
questions.answer: A - hydrogen fluoride only
steps: F- is the weakest reducing agent of the halides, so it is not oxidised by concentrated H2SO4.
NaF + H2SO4 -> NaHSO4 + HF is a non-redox reaction.
No fluorine (F2) or sulfur dioxide is formed.
Answer A.

questions.question: Some data for three small molecules are shown. Explain the large variation in boiling temperatures, given the small range in Mr values. Detailed descriptions of the forces are not required.
questions.answer: The data table for the three molecules is not in the text; check the PDF before writing the explanation

questions.question: Calcium chloride is soluble in water. Complete the diagram to show how water molecules interact with each ion.
questions.answer: Needs the diagram from the PDF; expected: O ends of water face Ca2+ and H ends face Cl-

questions.question: Explain why bromine is a liquid but iodine is a solid at room temperature. Detailed explanations of the forces are not required.
questions.answer: Both are simple molecular, but I2 has more electrons, so stronger London (induced dipole) forces hold its molecules together, needing more energy to melt or boil
steps: Bromine and iodine are simple molecular substances with weak London (instantaneous dipole-induced dipole) forces between molecules.
An I2 molecule has more electrons (106) than a Br2 molecule (70) and is larger, so it is more polarisable.
Stronger intermolecular forces in I2 need more energy to overcome, so it has a higher melting and boiling temperature.
I2 is solid at room temperature, while Br2 has weaker forces, so it is a liquid.

questions.question: Which statement about chlorine, bromine and iodine is not correct? A boiling temperature increases down the group; B reactivity increases down the group; C first ionisation energy decreases down the group; D electronegativity decreases down the group.
questions.answer: B - reactivity increases down the group (this is wrong; reactivity decreases)
steps: Boiling temperature increases down Group 7 (A is correct) because London forces increase with size.
Reactivity decreases down Group 7 (oxidising power falls), so B is the incorrect statement.
First ionisation energy decreases down the group (C is correct) as atoms get larger.
Electronegativity decreases down the group (D is correct). Answer B.

questions.topic: Products Of KBr With Sulfuric Acid
questions.question: Solid potassium bromide reacts with concentrated sulfuric acid. Which of these substances does not form? A bromine, B hydrogen bromide, C hydrogen sulfide, D sulfur dioxide.
questions.answer: C - hydrogen sulfide
steps: Br- is a moderate reducing agent, so it is oxidised to Br2 and H2SO4 is reduced to SO2.
HBr is formed as the first product (non-redox step), so it is a product.
Bromine (A), HBr (B) and SO2 (D) are all products.
H2S requires a stronger reducing agent such as I-, so it does not form with KBr. Answer C.

questions.question: When iodine dissolves in a non-polar organic solvent, the solution formed is: A purple, B orange, C colourless, D brown.
questions.answer: A - purple
steps: Iodine is non-polar and dissolves well in non-polar solvents such as hexane or cyclohexane.
The iodine molecules in a non-polar solvent give a purple (violet) solution.
Iodine in water gives a brown solution, which is different.
Answer A.

questions.question: Which silver halides are soluble in concentrated aqueous ammonia? A AgBr and AgI, B AgCl and AgI, C AgCl and AgBr, D AgCl only.
questions.answer: C - AgCl and AgBr
steps: AgCl dissolves in dilute and concentrated ammonia.
AgBr dissolves only in concentrated ammonia.
AgI does not dissolve in aqueous ammonia.
So the pair soluble in concentrated ammonia is AgCl and AgBr: answer C.

questions.question: Which of these increases as Group 7 is descended? A oxidising ability of the molecular halogens, B reducing ability of the halide ions, C electrostatic attraction between the nucleus and outer electrons, D electronegativity of the halogen atoms.
questions.answer: B - reducing ability of the halide ions
steps: Oxidising ability of the halogens decreases down the group (A is wrong).
Reducing ability of the halide ions increases down the group (B is correct).
Attraction between nucleus and outer electrons decreases down the group (C is wrong).
Electronegativity decreases down the group (D is wrong). Answer B.

questions.question: Which sequence shows the molecules in order of increasing boiling temperature? A H2O < Br2 < Cl2 < CH4, B Br2 < CH4 < Cl2 < H2O, C Cl2 < CH4 < H2O < Br2, D CH4 < Cl2 < Br2 < H2O.
questions.answer: D - CH4 < Cl2 < Br2 < H2O
steps: Approximate boiling temperatures: CH4 -162 C, Cl2 -34 C, Br2 +59 C, H2O +100 C.
Cl2 and Br2 are held by London forces, which increase with the number of electrons.
H2O has hydrogen bonds, giving the highest boiling temperature of the four.
Order CH4 < Cl2 < Br2 < H2O: answer D.

questions.question: Aqueous chlorine is added to aqueous potassium iodide, a non-polar organic solvent is added and the mixture shaken. What colour is seen in the organic layer? A brown, B green, C orange, D violet.
questions.answer: D - violet
steps: Chlorine oxidises iodide ions to iodine: Cl2 + 2I- -> 2Cl- + I2.
Iodine is extracted into the non-polar organic solvent.
Iodine in a non-polar solvent gives a violet (purple) colour.
Answer D.

questions.question: Use trends in Group 7 to predict the colour and physical state of astatine at room temperature.
questions.answer: Black (dark) solid
steps: Colour darkens down Group 7: F2 pale yellow, Cl2 green, Br2 red-brown, I2 grey-black solid.
Melting and boiling temperatures increase down the group, so astatine is solid at room temperature.
Extrapolating the trend, astatine is a dark (black) solid.

questions.question: State the meaning of the term electronegativity.
questions.answer: The tendency or power of an atom to attract the bonding pair of electrons in a covalent bond
steps: Electronegativity is a property of an atom in a covalent bond.
It is the measure of the atom's power to attract a shared (bonding) pair of electrons towards itself.

questions.question: Explain the trend in electronegativity down Group 7.
questions.answer: Electronegativity decreases down the group because the atoms get larger and have more shielding, so the bonding pair is held less strongly by the nucleus
steps: Going down Group 7, the number of electron shells increases.
The atomic radius increases and the outer electrons are shielded more by inner shells.
The attraction between the nucleus and the bonding pair of electrons is therefore weaker.
So the electronegativity decreases down the group.

questions.topic: Reactions Of Chlorine With Water And Alkali
questions.question: Compare and contrast the reactions of chlorine with water, cold dilute aqueous alkali and hot concentrated aqueous alkali. Include an equation for each reaction, state the type of reaction and the oxidation numbers of chlorine. State symbols are not required.
questions.answer: All three are disproportionation (Cl 0 is reduced to -1 and oxidised); water gives HCl and HClO, cold dilute alkali gives NaCl and NaClO, hot concentrated alkali gives NaCl and NaClO3 (Cl +5)
steps: Water: Cl2 + H2O -> HCl + HClO; Cl goes 0 -> -1 (HCl) and 0 -> +1 (HClO); disproportionation; a weak, reversible reaction that gives an acidic mixture.
Cold dilute NaOH: Cl2 + 2NaOH -> NaCl + NaClO + H2O; Cl 0 -> -1 (NaCl) and 0 -> +1 (NaClO); disproportionation; forms bleach.
Hot concentrated NaOH: 3Cl2 + 6NaOH -> NaClO3 + 5NaCl + 3H2O; Cl 0 -> -1 and 0 -> +5 (NaClO3); disproportionation.
Contrast: the same type of reaction in all three, but the product depends on temperature and concentration of the alkali.
Contrast: cold dilute alkali gives chlorate(I), ClO-, at +1, while hot concentrated alkali gives chlorate(V), ClO3-, at +5.
Chlorine is therefore both oxidised and reduced in each case (Cl2 is the element with oxidation number 0).

questions.question: Which reaction is not a disproportionation? A 3Cl2 + 6NaOH -> NaClO3 + 5NaCl + 3H2O, B 2H2O2 -> 2H2O + O2, C Cl2 + H2O -> HCl + HClO, D Zn + CuSO4 -> ZnSO4 + Cu.
questions.answer: D - Zn + CuSO4 -> ZnSO4 + Cu
steps: A: Cl goes from 0 to -1 and +5, so it is disproportionation.
B: O goes from -1 to 0 and -2, so it is disproportionation.
C: Cl goes from 0 to -1 and +1, so it is disproportionation.
D: Zn is oxidised and Cu2+ is reduced by different species: a displacement (redox) reaction, not disproportionation. Answer D.

questions.question: Four tests: 1 flame test, 2 acidified barium nitrate, 3 acidified silver nitrate, 4 NaOH then testing gas with indicator paper. Which tests could be used to positively identify the ions in ammonium chloride? A 1 and 2, B 1 and 3, C 2 and 4, D 3 and 4.
questions.answer: D - 3 and 4
steps: Test 3 with acidified silver nitrate gives a white precipitate of AgCl, positively identifying Cl-.
Test 4 with NaOH gives NH3 gas, which turns damp red litmus blue, positively identifying NH4+.
Test 1 gives no flame colour for NH4+ and test 2 does not identify Cl- or NH4+.
Answer D.

questions.question: Descending Group 7 from fluorine to iodine, electronegativity decreases even though nuclear charge increases. Explain the trend in electronegativity.
questions.answer: The number of electron shells increases and shielding increases, so the nuclear attraction for the bonding pair falls even though the nuclear charge rises
steps: Nuclear charge increases down the group, which would increase attraction.
However, atoms gain more electron shells, so atomic radius increases.
Inner shells shield the outer electrons from the nucleus more strongly.
The bonding pair is therefore attracted less strongly, so electronegativity decreases.

questions.question: Iodate(V) ions react with iodide ions in acid solution: IO3- + 5I- + 6H+ -> 3I2 + 3H2O. Explain, in terms of oxidation numbers of iodine in the three species, why this is not a disproportionation reaction. (The PDF text is partly garbled; the expected wording appears to be 'not a disproportionation reaction'.)
questions.answer: Two different iodine species change: IO3- (I = +5) is reduced to I2 (0) and I- (I = -1) is oxidised to I2 (0); one species is not both oxidised and reduced, so it is not disproportionation
steps: In IO3-, iodine is +5; in I- it is -1; in I2 it is 0.
IO3- goes from +5 to 0, so it is reduced.
I- goes from -1 to 0, so it is oxidised.
Iodine from two different reactants is converted into the same product, so this is comproportionation (the reverse of disproportionation), not disproportionation.

questions.topic: Sulfur Product With Lowest Oxidation Number
questions.question: Hydrogen bromide and hydrogen iodide reduce sulfuric acid. Identify, by name or formula, the compound containing sulfur with its lowest oxidation number in that reaction.
questions.answer: Hydrogen sulfide, H2S (sulfur at -2)
steps: Sulfur in H2SO4 is +6; in SO2 it is +4; in elemental S it is 0; in H2S it is -2.
HI is the stronger reducing agent and reduces H2SO4 all the way to H2S.
H2S has sulfur at -2, the lowest oxidation number formed.
Answer: H2S.

questions.question: Explain the trend in boiling temperatures of the hydrogen halides (HF, HCl, HBr, HI), as shown in a graph in the PDF.
questions.answer: HF has the highest boiling temperature because of hydrogen bonding; from HCl to HI the boiling temperature rises because the number of electrons and the size of the molecules increase, so London forces increase
steps: HF has hydrogen bonds between molecules (H bonded to the very electronegative F), so it has an unusually high boiling temperature.
HCl, HBr and HI have only permanent dipole and London forces.
Going from HCl to HI, the number of electrons increases, so the London (van der Waals) forces get stronger.
More energy is needed to overcome the stronger forces, so the boiling temperature increases from HCl to HI.

questions.question: A sample of seawater was evaporated; the residue of mass 0.098 g was dissolved and excess AgNO3 added. The AgCl precipitate weighed 0.226 g. Calculate the percentage by mass of chloride ions in the solid residue.
steps: Each AgCl contains one Cl-, so moles Cl- = 1.58 x 10^-3 mol.
Percentage by mass = 0.0560 / 0.098 x 100 = 57.1%.

questions.question: Which trend is not correct as Group 7 is descended? A atomic radius increases, B boiling temperature increases, C electronegativity decreases, D reactivity increases.
questions.answer: D - reactivity increases (reactivity decreases)
steps: Atomic radius increases down Group 7 (A is correct).
Boiling temperature increases down Group 7 (B is correct).
Electronegativity decreases down Group 7 (C is correct).
Reactivity decreases down Group 7, so statement D is the incorrect trend.

questions.topic: Products Of NaBr With Sulfuric Acid
questions.question: When sodium bromide reacts with concentrated sulfuric acid, sodium hydrogensulfate is always formed. What other products are formed? A hydrogen bromide only, B bromine and hydrogen bromide only, C bromine, hydrogen bromide and sulfur dioxide only, D bromine, hydrogen bromide, sulfur dioxide and sulfur only.
questions.answer: C - bromine, hydrogen bromide and sulfur dioxide only
steps: NaBr + H2SO4 -> NaHSO4 + HBr: the first, non-redox step gives HBr.
Concentrated H2SO4 is strong enough to oxidise some of the HBr to Br2, reducing itself to SO2 (S from +6 to +4).
No elemental sulfur or H2S forms with bromide (these need iodide).
Answer C.

questions.question: A fixed amount of concentrated H2SO4 is reacted separately with an excess of four solid potassium halides. In which reaction would the greatest number of moles of halide be oxidised? Options are in the PDF.

questions.question: A 2.49 g mixture of KI and KCl gave 0.162 g of dried solid in the analysis. Calculate the percentage by mass of KI. Ar: Ag 107.9, K 39.1, I 126.9.

questions.question: MnO2(s) + 4HCl(aq) -> MnCl2(aq) + Cl2(g) + 2H2O(l). Show, by reference to oxidation numbers, that this is a redox reaction.
questions.answer: Mn goes from +4 to +2 (reduced); Cl goes from -1 in HCl to 0 in Cl2 (oxidised), so it is redox
steps: Mn in MnO2 is +4 (O = -2 each); in MnCl2 it is +2.
Mn decreases from +4 to +2, so MnO2 is reduced.
Cl in HCl is -1; in Cl2 it is 0.
Cl increases from -1 to 0, so chloride is oxidised: both oxidation and reduction occur.

questions.question: Chlorine gas is bubbled through aqueous potassium iodide to form iodine. Hexane is then added and the mixture shaken, forming two layers. State the colour of each layer.
questions.answer: Aqueous layer: colourless (or very pale); hexane layer: purple (violet)
steps: Chlorine oxidises I- to I2 in the aqueous solution: Cl2 + 2I- -> 2Cl- + I2.
Iodine is much more soluble in hexane than water, so most of it moves into the hexane layer.
The aqueous layer therefore becomes colourless or very pale.
The hexane (top, less dense) layer is purple (violet) with the iodine.

questions.topic: Iodine Solubility In Hexane Versus Water
questions.question: Explain why iodine is more soluble in hexane than in water, by considering the intermolecular forces in iodine, hexane and water and any intermolecular forces formed between iodine and the solvents. Detailed descriptions of how the forces form are not required.
questions.answer: Iodine and hexane are both non-polar and interact by London forces, which replace the London forces broken in iodine and hexane; water has strong hydrogen bonds that iodine cannot replace, so iodine dissolves less in water
steps: Iodine is a simple molecular, non-polar substance held together by London (instantaneous dipole-induced dipole) forces.
Hexane is non-polar and has only London forces between its molecules.
Iodine and hexane can form London forces between them that are similar in strength to those already present, so little energy is needed.
Water has strong hydrogen bonds between its molecules, which must be broken to make room for iodine.
Iodine cannot form hydrogen bonds with water, and the iodine-water forces are weak, so the energy cost is not compensated.
So iodine is much more soluble in hexane (like dissolves like).

questions.answer: The option equations are not in the text; check the PDF (expected: a less reactive halogen displacing a more reactive halide, e.g. Br2 + 2Cl-)

questions.question: What are the gaseous products, other than water vapour, formed when concentrated sulfuric acid is added to potassium bromide? A bromine and sulfur dioxide only, B bromine, hydrogen bromide and hydrogen sulfide only, C bromine, hydrogen bromide and sulfur dioxide only, D bromine, hydrogen bromide, sulfur dioxide and hydrogen sulfide only.
questions.answer: C - bromine, hydrogen bromide and sulfur dioxide only
steps: KBr gives HBr, which is partly oxidised to Br2 by concentrated H2SO4.
The H2SO4 is reduced to SO2 (S +6 to +4).
H2S is not formed with bromide ions, which are not reducing enough.
Answer C.

questions.question: When chlorine reacts with hot concentrated potassium hydroxide it disproportionates. What are the oxidation states of chlorine in the products? A -1 and +3, B -1 and +5, C +1 and -1, D +1 and +5.
questions.answer: B - -1 and +5
steps: Hot concentrated alkali forms chloride (Cl-, -1) and chlorate (ClO3-, +5).
3Cl2 + 6KOH -> 5KCl + KClO3 + 3H2O.
Chlorine goes from 0 to -1 (reduction) and 0 to +5 (oxidation).
Answer B.

questions.question: Which test shows that sodium chloride solution contains chloride ions? A damp blue litmus turns red, B damp blue litmus is bleached, C dilute hydrochloric acid followed by silver nitrate gives a white precipitate, D dilute nitric acid followed by silver nitrate gives a white precipitate.
questions.answer: D - dilute nitric acid followed by silver nitrate gives a white precipitate
steps: Acidify with dilute nitric acid, not hydrochloric acid, because HCl would add chloride ions and give a false positive.
Add silver nitrate: a white precipitate of AgCl shows chloride ions.
A and B describe tests for acid or bleach, not chloride.
Answer D.

questions.question: The boiling temperatures of the halogens increase down Group 7 because on descending the group the: A bond polarities increase, B covalent bond strengths increase, C electronegativities increase, D number of electrons in the molecule increases.
questions.answer: D - number of electrons in the molecule increases
steps: Halogens are simple molecular substances held together by London forces between molecules.
Down the group, molecules get larger and have more electrons.
More electrons give stronger London forces, so more energy is needed to boil them.
Covalent bond strengths and electronegativities are not the reason; answer D.

questions.question: Bromine and chlorine each have two stable isotopes. Which statement is true? A the atomic radius of 81Br is greater than that of 79Br, B the electronegativity of 35Cl is greater than that of 37Cl, C the first ionisation energy of 37Cl is greater than that of 79Br, D the mass spectrum of CH2BrCl has two molecular ion peaks.
questions.answer: C - the first ionisation energy of 37Cl is greater than that of 79Br
steps: Isotopes have the same electronic structure, so they have the same atomic radius (A is false) and electronegativity (B is false).
Cl is above Br in Group 7, so the first ionisation energy of Cl is greater than that of Br (C is true).
CH2BrCl has several molecular ion peaks from the combinations of 35/37 Cl and 79/81 Br, not just two (D is false).
Answer C.

questions.question: Which solution remains clear on addition of barium chloride solution? A dilute sulfuric acid, B silver nitrate solution, C sodium nitrate solution, D sodium sulfate solution.
questions.answer: C - sodium nitrate solution
steps: Dilute sulfuric acid gives a white precipitate of BaSO4 with BaCl2 (A forms a precipitate).
Silver nitrate gives a white precipitate of AgCl with BaCl2 (B forms a precipitate).
Sodium sulfate gives a white precipitate of BaSO4 (D forms a precipitate).
Sodium nitrate gives no precipitate with barium chloride, so it stays clear. Answer C.

questions.question: Which substance is formed when concentrated sulfuric acid reacts with potassium chloride? A Cl2, B S, C H2S, D KHSO4.
questions.answer: D - KHSO4
steps: Cl- is not oxidised by concentrated H2SO4 (it is too weak a reducing agent), so Cl2, S and H2S are not formed.
The reaction is a non-redox acid-displacement: H2SO4 + KCl -> KHSO4 + HCl.
The hydrogensulfate salt KHSO4 is formed.
Answer D.

questions.question: Silver nitrate forms a white precipitate with an aqueous solution of an unknown ionic compound, and a flame test gives a red flame. The compound could be: A calcium iodide, B lithium bromide, C potassium carbonate, D strontium chloride.
questions.answer: D - strontium chloride
steps: A red flame points to Sr2+ or Li+, so A (Ca, brick red) and C (K, lilac) are unlikely.
B (lithium bromide) would give a cream precipitate with AgNO3, not a white one.
SrCl2 gives a red flame and a white precipitate of AgCl with AgNO3.
Answer D.

questions.question: What is the colour of the solution formed when iodine dissolves in cyclohexane? A blue-black, B grey, C purple, D yellow.
questions.answer: C - purple
steps: Iodine is non-polar and dissolves in non-polar cyclohexane.
Iodine in a non-polar solvent gives a purple (violet) solution.
Blue-black is the colour of iodine in starch, not in cyclohexane.
Answer C.

questions.question: Which row shows the correct trends down the group for the elements of Group 7? The table of rows (A to D) is in the PDF.
questions.answer: The table of rows is not in the text; check the PDF (expected: radius up, electronegativity down, reactivity down, boiling temperature up)

questions.question: Cyclohexane (density 0.78 g cm-3) and aqueous iodine (density above 1.0 g cm-3) are shaken and left to stand. What colours are the two layers that form?
questions.answer: Top layer (cyclohexane) purple/violet; bottom layer (aqueous) pale, colourless or yellow-brown
steps: Cyclohexane is less dense than water (0.78 g cm-3), so it forms the top layer.
Iodine is much more soluble in cyclohexane, so it moves into the top layer and gives it a purple (violet) colour.
The aqueous layer below is left pale (colourless or only slightly yellow-brown) once most iodine has been extracted.
So: top layer purple, bottom layer pale or colourless.

questions.question: Which is a displacement reaction that results in a visible colour change in solution? Options are in the PDF.
questions.answer: The option reactions are not in the text; check the PDF (expected: chlorine displacing bromide, giving orange/brown bromine)

questions.question: When chlorine water is added to potassium bromide solution, a pale brown colour is seen. Write an ionic equation for this reaction. State symbols are not required.
questions.answer: Cl2 + 2Br- -> 2Cl- + Br2
steps: Chlorine is more reactive than bromine, so it displaces bromine from bromide.
Br- is oxidised to Br2 (pale brown in water), and Cl2 is reduced to Cl-.
Ionic equation: Cl2 + 2Br- -> 2Cl- + Br2.

questions.question: Cl2(g) + H2O(l) -> HClO(aq) + HCl(aq). By considering oxidation numbers, show that this equation represents a disproportionation reaction.
questions.answer: Cl goes from 0 in Cl2 to +1 in HClO (oxidised) and to -1 in HCl (reduced), so chlorine is both oxidised and reduced in the same reaction
steps: Cl in Cl2 is 0.
In HClO, Cl is +1 (H = +1, O = -2), so it is oxidised.
In HCl, Cl is -1, so it is reduced.
The same element is both oxidised and reduced, so this is disproportionation.

questions.topic: Non-Redox Reaction Of KCl With Sulfuric Acid
questions.question: The equation H2SO4 + KCl -> HCl + KHSO4 is shown. State why this is not a redox reaction.
questions.answer: No element changes oxidation number: S stays +6, Cl stays -1, K stays +1, H stays +1, O stays -2
steps: Check each element: S is +6 in H2SO4 and in KHSO4; H is +1 throughout.
Cl is -1 in KCl and in HCl; K is +1 in KCl and KHSO4.
O is -2 throughout.
No oxidation number changes, so there is no electron transfer and it is not redox.

questions.topic: Ionic Equation Iodide And Sulfuric Acid
questions.question: Combine the half-equations 2I- -> I2 + 2e- and 8H+ + H2SO4 + 8e- -> H2S + 4H2O to deduce the ionic equation for the reaction between iodide ions and concentrated sulfuric acid.
steps: Multiply the iodide half-equation by 4 to give 8I- -> 4I2 + 8e-.
Add the sulfuric acid half-equation: 8H+ + H2SO4 + 8e- -> H2S + 4H2O.
Cancel the 8 electrons on each side.
Result: 8I- + 8H+ + H2SO4 -> 4I2 + H2S + 4H2O.

questions.topic: Chloride Versus Iodide With Sulfuric Acid
questions.question: Explain the difference in the reaction of concentrated sulfuric acid with chloride ions and with iodide ions.
questions.answer: Iodide is a strong enough reducing agent to reduce concentrated H2SO4 (to SO2, S or H2S) and be oxidised to I2, but chloride is too weak a reducing agent and only gives HCl
steps: Chloride ions are weak reducing agents, so they cannot reduce H2SO4; only HCl forms by acid displacement.
Iodide ions are much stronger reducing agents, so they are oxidised to I2 and H2SO4 is reduced to H2S (or SO2).
The difference is the reducing power of the halide ion, which increases down the group.

questions.topic: Role Of Sulfuric Acid With Iodide
questions.question: Concentrated sulfuric acid reacts with sodium iodide. What is one role of the sulfuric acid? A oxidising agent, B reducing agent, C proton acceptor, D lone pair donor.
questions.answer: A - oxidising agent
steps: H2SO4 is reduced (S goes from +6 to lower oxidation numbers such as H2S or SO2).
A species that is reduced is an oxidising agent, so H2SO4 acts as an oxidising agent.
I- is oxidised to I2, so iodide acts as the reducing agent.
Answer A.

questions.topic: Iodine In Hexane With Potassium Chloride
questions.question: An aqueous solution of potassium chloride is added to a solution of iodine in hexane and shaken. After a time two layers form. What is the colour of each layer?
questions.answer: Top hexane layer purple (violet); bottom aqueous layer colourless (no reaction, iodine stays in hexane)
steps: Hexane has a lower density than water, so the hexane layer forms the top layer.
Iodine is more soluble in hexane than in water, and chloride ions do not oxidise iodine, so no reaction occurs.
The iodine remains in the hexane, which is purple (violet).
The aqueous (bottom) layer contains only KCl and is colourless.
